sheet.howExamined: C1, 1 hour, 60 marks at Foundation and 70 at Higher, with a calculator and the Chemistry Data Leaflet. Isotopes come inside the atomic structure question: a two-mark definition, particle counts for two isotopes, a comparison, and at Higher a three-mark relative atomic mass (top line, divide by 100, answer to 1 decimal place). Summer 2025's six-mark QWC asked for the definition, the particles' positions and the counts for chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
traps: Isotopes defined as a single atom instead of atoms, in the plural (Summer 2025 C1 H Q2)
Electrons brought into the definition of isotopes, or 'the same element' given without the atomic number or protons (Summer 2025 C1 F Q2)
The particle counts of two isotopes muddled, with the heavier one given extra protons or electrons (Summer 2025 C1 F Q2)

A relative atomic mass with an isotope missing from the top line, or never divided by 100 (Summer 2023 C1 H Q1)
An answer not rounded to the one decimal place the question instructed (Summer 2025 C1 H Q6)

Silicon has three isotopes. The table gives their percentage abundances.

steps.working: Multiply each mass number by its abundance: 28 × 92.2 = 2581.6, 29 × 4.7 = 136.3, 30 × 3.1 = 93.
steps.decision: Every isotope goes into the top line. Leaving one out was the commonest slip in the Summer 2023 relative atomic mass question.

The abundances are percentages, so the total is for 100 atoms. Stopping at 2810.9 leaves the mass of 100 atoms, not the mean.

options: Because the abundances are percentages, so the top line is the mass of 100 atoms
Because relative atomic masses are always small
whyMenu.explain: Percentages are out of 100, so dividing by 100 turns the total for 100 atoms into the mean for one.

steps.decision: The stem asks for 1 decimal place, so 28.109 is written 28.1. Check: it lies between 28 and 30, close to 28, the commonest isotope. A plain average of the three mass numbers, 29, would count the rare isotopes as heavily as silicon-28.

workedExamples.stem:
Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are two atoms of carbon, atomic number 6.
(a) How many protons, neutrons and electrons does each atom have? [2]
(b) Explain why the two atoms are isotopes. [2]

steps.working: Protons: both have 6, the atomic number. Electrons: both have 6, because an atom has as many electrons as protons.
steps.decision: The atomic number is on both symbols, so protons and electrons are the same for both.
Mass number take away atomic number for each. Writing 14 for carbon-14 counts the protons twice.

steps.working: Both are carbon atoms, with the same atomic number, 6.
steps.decision: The first half of the definition, tied to the atomic number rather than to 'the same element' alone.

steps.working: They have different mass numbers, 12 and 14, because they have different numbers of neutrons, 6 and 8.
steps.decision: The second half: the difference is in the neutrons. Electrons play no part in the definition.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) Carbon-12: 6 protons, 6 neutrons, 6 electrons; carbon-14: 6 protons, 8 neutrons, 6 electrons. (b) They have the same atomic number (6 protons) but different mass numbers, because their numbers of neutrons differ.

items.stem: What does the atomic number of an element count?

options.feedback: Protons only. It is the number that stays fixed for every atom of an element.
Neutrons can vary between atoms of one element, which is the whole of this lesson. The atomic number counts protons.

options.text: the protons and neutrons in one atom
options.feedback: That is the mass number. The atomic number counts protons alone.

items.stem: An atom has mass number 23 and atomic number 11. How many neutrons does it have?

options.feedback: 23 − 11 = 12: mass number take away atomic number.
23 counts protons and neutrons together; take the 11 protons away.
That adds the two numbers. The protons are already inside the 23, so subtract.

items.stem: What is the mean of 35 and 37?
items.skill: Prerequisite from mathematics; you are not expected to have met relative atomic mass yet

options.feedback: 35 + 37 = 72, and 72 ÷ 2 = 36. This lesson shows why chlorine's relative atomic mass is not simply this plain mean.
That is the total. Divide by the two values to get the mean: 36.
That is the difference between them. The mean is halfway: 36.

options.feedback: Plural, same protons, different neutrons: both marks.

options.feedback: Isotopes differ in neutrons. Bringing electrons in cost the mark in Summer 2025.

options.text: atoms of different elements with the same mass number
options.feedback: Isotopes are one element, so the same atomic number, with different mass numbers. This description has both halves the wrong way round.

items.stem: Which statement about chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 is correct?
items.skill: Compare the particles in two isotopes

options.text: both have 17 protons and 17 electrons; chlorine-37 has two more neutrons
options.feedback: 18 neutrons against 20; everything else is the same.
19 protons would make it a different element, potassium. The extra mass is in the neutrons.
Both atoms have as many electrons as protons, 17. The extra mass is in the neutrons.

options.text: they have the same number of neutrons
options.feedback: Their neutrons are exactly what differs: 18 and 20.

items.stem: Potassium is 93.3% potassium-39 and 6.7% potassium-41. Which is its relative atomic mass?

options.feedback: Between 39 and 41 and very close to 39, the isotope that makes up nearly all of the sample.
That is the plain average of 39 and 41, as if the isotopes were equally common. Weight each by its abundance.
That pairs each abundance with the other isotope, putting the answer near the rare one. It should sit near 39.
That is the top line, the mass of 100 atoms. Divide by 100.

items.stem: Why is the relative atomic mass of chlorine 35.5 and not a whole number?
items.skill: Explain a relative atomic mass as a weighted mean of isotopes

options.text: chlorine is a mixture of isotopes, and the value is their mean weighted by abundance
options.feedback: A weighted mean of 35 and 37, pulled towards 35 because that isotope is three times as common.

options.text: it is the plain average of 35 and 37
options.feedback: The plain average is 36. The real value is lower because chlorine-35 is far more common.

options.text: some chlorine atoms contain half a neutron
options.feedback: Particles only come whole. The half appears when two kinds of whole atom are averaged.

items.stem: For boron: 10 × 20 + 11 × 80 = 1080. What is the next step?

options.feedback: The abundances are percentages, so divide by 100.
That is the mass of 100 atoms. The relative atomic mass must lie between 10 and 11.
Dividing by the number of isotopes is the plain-average habit. The top line is for 100 atoms, so divide by 100.

indicativeContent.point: Isotopes are atoms of one element that share an atomic number (the same number of protons).
Isotopes have different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons).
Protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus.
Electrons are found in shells around the nucleus.
Both isotopes have 3 protons and 3 electrons.

scheme.for: a banded answer covering the definition of isotopes (same atomic number, different mass number or neutrons), the positions of the particles (protons and neutrons in the nucleus, electrons in shells), and the counts: both isotopes 3 protons and 3 electrons, lithium-6 3 neutrons, lithium-7 4 neutrons
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Three bullet points, in order.
Numbers for both isotopes, not just one.
parts.workedSolution: Isotopes are atoms of one element that have the same atomic number, and so the same number of protons, but different mass numbers, because their numbers of neutrons differ. In an atom the protons and neutrons are found in the nucleus, and the electrons are in shells around the nucleus. Lithium-6 and lithium-7 both have 3 protons and 3 electrons, because lithium's atomic number is 3. Lithium-6 has 6 − 3 = 3 neutrons, while lithium-7 has 7 − 3 = 4 neutrons, one more than lithium-6.

findTheMistake.stem:
Tomás works out sulfur's relative atomic mass from sulfur-32 (95%), sulfur-33 (0.8%) and sulfur-34 (4.2%), and is asked for 1 decimal place. [3]
His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The top line is complete and added correctly, with all three isotopes in it. The last line stops there: 3209.2 is the mass of 100 atoms, because the abundances are percentages. Dividing by 100 gives 32.092, which is 32.1 to 1 decimal place. An answer far above every mass number is the sign to look for.
findTheMistake.feedback: One of the three marks, for the top line. The Summer 2023 report names this slip. Every relative atomic mass lies between its isotopes' mass numbers, so 3209.2 for sulfur should have stopped you.
